headline: Okasu, “to invade”, is a doublet of 犯す (okasu, “to commit (crime)”) and 冒す (okasu, “to risk”).
アラブ is an internationalism, ultimately from Arabic, first cited in Japanese in a 1914 dictionary of loanwords.
Satsujin is 殺 (satsu, “killing”) plus 人 (jin, “human”).
Maneki is the continuative stem of the verb 招く (maneku, “to invite, call over”).
Zai, “fortune”, is from Middle Chinese 財 (MC dzoj).
Susugu was originally pronounced unvoiced, as 濯く (susuku).
Shūshū is from Middle Chinese 收集, first appearing around 760 CE with the spelling 聚集 in kanbun texts.
Men suru is 面 (men, “face”) plus する (-suru).
Azawarau is 嘲 (aza, “something off-color or not quite right”) plus 笑う (warau, “laugh”).
Hachimitsu is 蜂 (hachi, “bee”) plus 蜜 (mitsu, “honey”).
インテリ is from the Russian word intelligéncija.
Torimodosu is 取る (toru, “to take”) plus 戻す (modosu, “to return, put back”).
Kinjiru is a shift from the verb 禁ずる (kinzuru), as -uru verbs moved to the -iru pattern.
Shōdaku is 承 (shō, “agree to”) plus 諾 (daku, “consent”).
Shotchū is possibly from 初中後 (shochūgo).
Yashiki is 屋 (ya, “house”) plus 敷 (shiki, “building site”), short for 敷地 (shikichi).
Kasen is 河 (ka, “river, large river”) plus 川 (sen, “river”).
Tsukusu is from Old Japanese, found in the Man'yōshū and spelled phonetically as 都久須.

term: デモンストレーション
headline: デモンストレーション is from English demonstration.
ショー is borrowed from English show.
Wataridori is 渡り (watari, the stem of 渡る (wataru, “to migrate”)) plus 鳥 (tori, “bird”).
Kokoromiru is 心 (kokoro, “heart, mind”) plus 見る (miru, “to look, watch, take care”).
Zadankai is, by surface analysis, 座談 (zadan) plus 会 (-kai).
Atsuryoku is 圧 (atsu, “pressure”) plus 力 (-ryoku, “power”).
Dōjō is from Middle Chinese 道場, literally “way + place”, itself originally a translation of a Sanskrit term for “seat of wisdom”.
ベストセラー is from English bestseller.
Kanten is 観 (kan, “to view”) plus 点 (ten, “point”).
Nae is from Old Japanese and is an apophonic form of 苗 (nawa, “seedling”).
Majieru is from Old Japanese 交ふ (mazifu), a lower bigrade verb.
Onozukara was originally 己 (ono, “oneself”) plus つ (tsu, possessive particle) plus 柄 (kara, “quality, characteristic”).
Oyaji is perhaps 親 (oya, “parent”) plus 父 (chichi, “father”), altered from an earlier form, oyachichi.
